title: Memory-Efficient Gradient Checkpointing for Large Models
problem: Training large language models requires storing all intermediate activations in GPU memory during forward propagation, creating a severe memory bottleneck. This memory requirement grows linearly with model depth and sequence length, limiting maximum trainable model sizes and batch sizes on available hardware.
motivation: Reducing GPU memory footprint during training enables scaling to larger models and batch sizes with limited hardware resources, directly improving training efficiency and accessibility.
method: This paper proposes using gradient checkpointing to train large models more efficiently: instead of storing all intermediate mathematical results (called activations) in GPU memory during the forward pass, the model forgets them immediately and recalculates them during the backward pass (when learning from mistakes). This strategy trades extra computation for substantial memory savings. The approach further optimizes by selectively deciding which intermediate results are worth saving and which to recalculate, plus scheduling the recalculation to minimize computational overhead.
key_novelty: The key innovation is selective gradient checkpointing that strategically chooses which intermediate results to save or recalculate by balancing memory savings against extra computational cost.
contributions: Novel gradient checkpointing algorithms for memory reduction
Memory-computation trade-off analysis for deep neural networks
Significant peak memory footprint reduction during LLM training
Training convergence guarantees with proposed checkpointing strategies
